lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Strong Starts, Mic-Drop Endings
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 7, Session 4
lesson.footer: Persuasive Speeches | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 7 Session 4

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA03 how spoken texts are organised into stages (opening and closing); VC2E5LY10 creating spoken texts for purpose and audience; VC2E5LY02 features of voice
plan.shape: first and last, model, practise, write: the first and last lines of famous speeches are compared, speech openings and endings are modelled, then students draft their own
plan.criticalFeature: the first 20 seconds decide whether they listen; the last line tells them exactly what to do next
decisionPoints: the choice check: the ending that lands
the exit board: a new mic-drop ending
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Say it. Today: start strong, finish stronger.
plan.catchUp: Missed earlier sessions? Openings and endings are taught from scratch; use your Week 5 issue.

routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Speech openings: a question, a story, a startling fact, Imagine..., who I am
Mic-drop ending: call to action + echo the opening + a short last line

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: sort openings and endings, rescue a fizzling ending, write mic-drop lines, then plan your own start and finish.

steps: Does it start something or finish it?

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we nail the first and last lines, the ones your audience remembers.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Write the opening moves and the mic-drop formula on the board.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write a speech opening that grabs the audience and an ending that tells them what to do.
successCriteria: I can name moves for opening and ending a speech.
I can write an ending with a clear call to action and a strong last line.
I can make my ending echo my opening.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Audiences remember the first line and the last line. Today we nail both.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we all start.
The second one is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 is reachable for all; SC2 is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 is the stretch.

slides.title: First lines, last lines
lines: Severn opened by saying who she was. Dr King ended with a vision.
Which do you remember: the middle, or the start and end?

notes.answer: the start and the end; that is where speakers put their best lines
beats: SAY: Think back over all four speeches.
What do you remember?
ASK: Do you remember the start and end,
or the middle? 1 start and end, 2 middle.
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: mostly 1
ASK: Tell your partner one first or last line you remember.
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: How dare you; I have a dream; please stop breaking it
SAY: The first 20 seconds earn attention. The last line tells them what to do.
trap: remembering a line but not where it came in the speech.
Fix: say speakers put their best lines first and last on purpose.
notes.prep: Low-coupling retrieval of Week 6 speakers. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: A short, powerful last line that leaves the audience with nothing more to say.
slides.example: Twenty steps is not a life.

notes.answer: a short, powerful last line that leaves the audience with nothing more to say
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Mic drop. Say it with me. Mic drop.
SAY: A short, powerful last line that leaves the audience with nothing more to say.
SAY: Twenty steps is not a life.
ASK: What makes a last line a mic drop?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: short; it echoes; it tells them what to do
trap: thinking a mic drop means a joke or a rude line.
Fix: say it is short and strong, and it fits the message.
notes.prep: Toolkit row 9: a call to action.

rows: a picture: Imagine walking twenty steps...
I'm a Year 6 student who has read The Last Bear.
Please fund wild polar bears instead.

notes.answer: an opening move; then action, an echo and a short last line
beats: POINT to Opening move.
SAY: In 20 seconds I want them picturing that bear. So I open with Imagine.
POINT to Ending: call to action.
SAY: Before I finish, they must know exactly what to do. Please fund wild bears.
POINT to Echo and Mic drop.
SAY: Then I bring back my opening picture. Twenty steps. Pause. Is not a life.
ASK: Say my mic drop with me, with the pause.
3 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: Twenty steps // is not a life.
trap: ending with thank you instead of the mic drop.
Fix: say thank you after the mic drop, if at all, after a pause.
notes.stretch: Make your mic drop five words or fewer.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: 20 seconds to earn attention; the last line says exactly what to do.

slides.title: Opening or ending?
slides.pivot: ask: does it pull them in, or tell them what to do?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which move is it?

items.text: Hands up if you've ever stepped on rubbish at the beach.
So on Friday, bring a seedling. Let's grow this.
Three years ago, our creek was full of frogs.
One bench. Nobody alone. Build it.
Imagine a lunchtime with no rubbish left behind.

say: One finger opening. Two fingers ending.
trap: calling every short line an ending.
Fix: ask does it ask them to do something? Student re-votes.
notes.help: Endings usually tell you what to do.

options.text: That's the end of my speech, thank you.
options.misconception: announces the end; asks the audience for nothing

options.text: Please walk to school on Monday. Your legs. Your planet.
Walking is good, I guess, and stuff.
options.misconception: fizzles: low modality and no action

notes.answer: B - a call to action, then a short punch
beats: SAY: Three last lines for a speech about walking to school.
ASK: Which ending lands best?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: perform B with a pause.
Less -> perform all three, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. They know what to do, and it lands short and strong.
trap: pointing to A because it's polite.
Fix: ask what will the audience do after A? Nothing.
notes.prep: Decision point before writing. Under 80% means the class writes one ending together.

slides.title: Start strong, finish stronger
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish by writing the opening and the ending of your speech, with an echo.

notes.answer: an opening move and an ending with action, echo and a short last line
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Your opening grabs them. Your ending sends them off to act.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: what will they DO after your last line? Does it echo your start?
ASK: Perform your opening and your last line for your partner.
45 sec each. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: a hook, then an action and a short echo
trap: an ending that adds a new reason.
Fix: student moves it into the middle of the speech.

notes.answer: e.g. Fix the taps. Thirsty kids can't think.

ASK: Write a mic-drop last line with a call to action.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your mic drop to your partner. Would it make them act?

notes.answer: open - yes, it tells them to switch off one light
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that your ending tells the audience what to do?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Read your mic drop to your partner. Would it make them act?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: yes, it tells them to switch off one light
